task_row_model.query: In Python, what is the difference between list.append() and list.extend()? When should I use each, and what are their time complexities? Give short examples.

documents.content: list.append(x) adds a single element x to the end of a list. If you pass a list to append, the entire list becomes one element nested at the end. list.extend(iterable) iterates over the iterable and adds each element to the list, so the elements are merged into the original list. Example: a = [1,2]; a.append([3,4]) -> [1,2,[3,4]]; a = [1,2]; a.extend([3,4]) -> [1,2,3,4]. This explains the difference in behavior but does not discuss performance in detail.

List comprehensions produce new lists by evaluating an expression for each item in an input sequence, often faster and more readable than using map with a lambda. For example, [x*2 for x in range(5)] yields [0,2,4,6,8]. map can be slightly more memory-efficient with iterators in Python 3 if you wrap results with list() or iterate lazily. Comprehensions are idiomatic for simple transformations, while map/filter can be useful when you already have reusable functions. This passage focuses on transformations rather than in-place list modification methods.

append() adds one object to the end of a list; extend() takes an iterable and adds each of its items to the list. Use append when you want to add a single element (including another list as a single element). Use extend when you want to concatenate another iterable’s elements into the list. Examples: a = [1]; a.append(2) -> [1,2]. b = [1]; b.extend([2,3]) -> [1,2,3]. Performance: append is amortized O(1) per call. extend is O(k) where k is the length of the iterable being added, because each element must be processed and appended. Note that using + to join lists creates a new list (O(n+m)).

The + operator concatenates lists by creating a new list with elements from both operands, while += (in-place extend) modifies the left-hand list when it supports in-place addition. For example, c = [1]; d = c + [2] returns a new list [1,2] leaving c unchanged; c += [2] modifies c to [1,2]. extend behaves like in-place concatenation: it iterates the right-hand iterable and appends items to the left-hand list. This passage emphasizes differences between concatenation and in-place modification, but it only indirectly covers single-element append behavior.

In JavaScript, array.push(item) appends one or more elements to the end of an array and returns the new length. pop() removes and returns the last element. These methods modify the array in place. Java's ArrayList.add(value) appends an element to the end and may resize the underlying array when capacity is exceeded. Both languages use similar dynamic array semantics, but method names and return values differ. This text compares push/pop and ArrayList.add rather than Python list methods and is focused on other languages' APIs.
